response.answer: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, renowned for her signature polka dots and immersive installations, died on August 14, 2026, at the age of 97 in Tokyo. Her work was exhibited globally, including at the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, and the Museum Ludwig. Kusama's art often featured repetitive motifs like dots, nets, and worms, and included notable pieces such as "Macaroni Girl," "The Visionary Flowers," and "Mirrored Corridor." Her death was confirmed by her studio without specifying the cause.

Repetitive motifs were her trademark, in various shapes, resembling netting, swirls or worms, but most often dots, dancing proudly on her canvases, or as sparkling balls or dots of light in her installations, in all their vibrant psychedelic glory. [...] By YURI KAGEYAMA

TOKYO (AP) — Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who splashed her signature polka dots on paintings, sculptures and museum installations around the world, has died, her studio said Thursday. She was 97.

Kusama died Aug. 14 at a hospital in Tokyo, Yayoi Kusama Studio said, without specifying the cause of death. [...] Over the years, Kusama made quirky but stunningly celebratory works like “Macaroni Girl,” a female figure plastered with macaroni, which expresses the fear of food; “The Visionary Flowers,” giant sculptures of twisting tulips, and “Mirrored Corridor,” a room with mirrors that delivers an illusion of a field of phallic protrusions speckled with dots.

She received the Order of Culture, Japan’s highest honour for artists, in 2016.

David Zwirner, an art dealer who represented Kusama for 15 years, said she “was without a doubt the most famous living artist in the world” at the time of her passing. # How Yayoi Kusama’s San Francisco triumph became an SFMOMA reckoning

By Tony Bravo, Arts & Culture ColumnistUpdated

Yayoi Kusama, pictured here in Tokyo, in 2012. The artist died on Aug. 14, at age 97.

Itsuo Inouye/Associated Press

For many Bay Area museumgoers, Yayoi Kusama’s first solo Northern California exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art in 2023 became the backdrop for selfies and Instagram reels. [...] Now, with news of Kusama’s death in Tokyo at 97 on Aug. 14, confirmed by the Yayoi Kusama Studio this week, the controversy that shadowed that SFMOMA show is inseparable from her local legacy.
